text: Course 3 covered the basic Update Set workflow: create one, make your changes, mark it complete, move it along. This lesson goes deeper into a question that workflow never answers: what should actually go inside an Update Set in the first place, once you're running six, ten, or twenty of them through a real release?

The instinct many new admins have is to batch Update Sets by day, or by developer. Both feel organized, but neither survives contact with a real release. A day-based set might bundle three unrelated fixes with no reason to travel together. The real convention is batching by feature or user story: everything needed to deliver one coherent piece of functionality goes in one Update Set, and nothing else does.

Splitting every small change into its own tiny Update Set sounds safer, but it backfires. If a login tweak, a related ACL fix, and a dependent business rule each live in separate sets, ServiceNow doesn't track or enforce the ordering between them. Promote them in the wrong sequence and you get preview errors, or worse, functionality that's silently broken. Across a release with forty tiny sets, that's a manual dependency puzzle someone has to solve correctly every time.

The opposite failure is just as common. One Update Set covering several unrelated features feels convenient while you're working, but it costs you later: if just one of those features turns out to have a bug after promotion, you cannot back out only that piece. Rolling back means rolling back everything welded into that set, including the features that were working fine.

Before marking an Update Set complete, ask two questions. Does everything in here serve one coherent piece of functionality? And could this set promote alone, without needing anything from another open Update Set? If either answer is no, fix the batching now — split out what doesn't belong, or finish the missing dependency before you close it.

Feature-sized batching costs a small amount of friction during development in exchange for an Update Set that can actually be promoted, reviewed, and rolled back on its own. Next up: what happens when the target instance doesn't agree with what's in your Update Set — resolving collisions.
